articles.title: Pokémon Polaroid Cameras Are Back Up for Preorder at Best Buy and Amazon Right Now
articles.summary: Preorders are live again for three new Pokémon-themed Polaroid instant cameras. Here's where they're available.
articles.body:
Here’s an unexpected crossover: Pokémon and Polaroid have teamed up to release a trio of pocket monster-themed instant cameras. There’s a yellow one based on Pikachu, complete with a lightning bolt tale; a pink-and-white Sylveon one with a ribbon-like strap; and a red-and-white one meant to evoke a Pokéball. They look great, but they're in and out of stock across major retailers (including Pokémon Center ).

As of today, you can check stock on Amazon , Best Buy , and Polaroid . If you see the one you want available, you'll want to order it fast.

Pokémon X Polaroid Instant Cameras and Film

Polaroid Go Generation 3 Mini Instant Camera - Pokémon Edition

Polaroid Go Generation 3 Mini Instant Camera - Pikachu Edition

Polaroid Go Generation 3 Mini Instant Camera - Pokémon Sylveon Edition

Polaroid Go Color Film Pokémon - Pikachu Edition (16 Photos)

Polaroid Go Color Film - Pokémon Sylveon Edition (16 Photos)

Polaroid Color I-Type Film - Pokémon Edition (8 Photos)

These are all Polaroid Now Generation 3 I-Type Instant Film Cameras, which means they're chunky and colorful, and they shoot full-size Polaroid pictures. The prints come out of the camera right after you take the photo. Polaroid also touts this model's "optimized exposures for sharper pictures."

Additionally, each camera has a self-timer mode, a tripod mount on the bottom, and battery life that lasts for 15 film packs.

While they're compatible with Polaroid i-Type film and Polaroid 600 film, Polaroid is also releasing a number of Pokémon-themed film packs. There's one to go along with each camera design. The Sylveon-themed film has a pink border with purple Sylveon and Pokéball silhouettes. Pikachu film has a yellow boarder, with three little Pikachus along the thick bottom side. Finally, the standard Pokémon Edition film has multiple designs, each one based on a popular Pokémon.

Again, if you're interested in picking up any of these items, you'll want to do it sooner than later. They seem to be quite popular and won't likely stay in stock for long.

Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

articles.title: ‘It’s Difficult To Justify the Investment’ – How MMORPGs Built (and Lost) the Live-Service Throne
articles.summary: How MMORPGs like World of Warcraft and EverQuest started the industry's obsession with never-ending live-service games.
articles.body:
Whatever happened to the MMORPG? In the early 2000s, the likes of World of Warcraft, RuneScape, and EverQuest dominated cyberspace, their worlds host to millions of players questing and raiding together. Today, Roblox’s titanic 123 million daily player count dwarfs the combined historical peak of this trio and many other genre stablemates of the time.

That’s not to say the MMORPG is dead. A brand new one, Aion 2 , launched just this week and quickly found itself on Steam’s Most Played list. The long-awaited Guild Wars 3 is on the horizon. And many of the genre’s pioneering games continue to run successfully, some even 25 years on from their inception. But that’s become the genre’s norm – ongoing projects built on ageing technology, rather than fresh new blood. The “live-service” game has taken its place, but that controversial industry trend has stolen the crown that the MMORPG forged.

Massively multiplayer online role-playing games were the first live-service games, long before the term had become common parlance. Both formats share a similar definition: at their core, they are online multiplayer games that are continually expanded, evolved, and developed beyond their initial launch, with that process often buffered by microtransactions or subscription models. The one key difference is that the modern live-service game can be anything from a tight 6v6 battle arena to a galaxy-spanning looter shooter. MMORPGs, meanwhile, typically take place in large fantasy or sci-fi open worlds, inspired by (or sometimes set in) the likes of Dungeons & Dragons or Star Wars, allowing players to act out long-imagined fantasies together.

Their replication of a world, with cities to visit and countries to travel across, means there’s an innate communal core to MMORPGs – like in reality, the game’s digital population becomes a community. It’s a notably different feeling compared to the communities of many modern live-service titles, like Apex Legends and Overwatch , which often focus on short, trigger-happy play cycles. People don’t admire Fortnite’s often rebranded islands in the same way they do World of Warcraft’s Nagrand or Stormwind. One is a battlefield, the other is home.

MMORPGs evolved from multi-user dungeons, or “MUDS”. Back in the early days of the internet, MUDs functioned like a virtual chatroom hinged around a fantastical adventure. They were D&D for your desktop instead of your tabletop. As entertaining as they were, multiplayer gaming took a huge step toward how we understand it today in 1997 when Ultima Online launched. It is the game from which the term ‘MMORPG’ came from, coined by Richard Garriott, creator of the Ultima series. Directed by Starr Long, it was an ambitious spin-off from the mainline Ultima RPG series that gave players something brand-new: a world that could change whilst they weren’t playing.

“The idea you could play in a virtual world with thousands of other people was a pretty novel idea at the time”, Long tells me. “It was like, ‘Wow, I can play D&D with my friends without even needing to be in the same town.’”

Ultima Online was one of the earliest pioneers of many aspects that are now baked into almost every live-service game, including monthly subscriptions and digital currency purchasable through brick-and-mortar retail stores. It became the first MMORPG to reach 100,000 subscribers and it did so within six months – an unexpected success which led to severe performance issues. Players responded by staging a digital protest in the castle grounds of Garriott’s in-game alter-ego, Lord British, over-indulging on consumables in order to fill the area with vomit.

“That was the turning point where we realized, while we are the game creators, this is the players’ world,” says Long. “We’re just facilitating it for them.”

The success of Ultima Online was analysed by many, including EverQuest co-creator Bill Trost. “The whole Ultima series was a big influence on me throughout high school,” he recalls. And in 1999, just two years after Ultima Online, Trost, alongside co-creators Steve Clover and Brad McQuaid, launched EverQuest. Its 3D game engine demonstrated just what an MMORPG world could be, and led to EverQuest’s immense popularity.

While EverQuest’s world looked significantly more advanced, Ultima Online’s success had taught Trost that the most important thing was the communal experience. “My world-building philosophy was to build a world with integrity, but don’t design it to death,” he explains. “The world we built and situations we set up made people bond together.”

Trost attributes EverQuest’s ongoing success to the team’s light touch, allowing players to make sense of the game themselves. It’s a sentiment echoed by Long: “We realized that running one of these games is more like running a government. Your people are your citizens,” he says.

These expansive communities changed people’s lives. It was in EverQuest where Jeff Kaplan first met Blizzard’s Vice President of Game Design, Rob Pardo, via the Legacy of Steel guild. That fateful meeting led to Kaplan joining the World of Warcraft team as a quest designer, a position from which he eventually rose to become game director.

Kaplan loved EverQuest, clocking up over 6,000 hours of play, but always felt like there could be more to the game. Joining the World of Warcraft team was his opportunity to make that “more” a reality. Blizzard needed something special because the competition was tough – it not only had to battle Ultima Online and EverQuest’s existing success, but stand up against the hype for EverQuest 2 and Star Wars: Galaxies, both of which were on the horizon when World of Warcraft launched in 2004.

“Everyone said, ‘Who is this RTS company? Who do they think they are to make an MMO?,” Kaplan recalls. At the time, Blizzard was known solely as a strategy games developer, although its Diablo ARPG series, beloved for its online multiplayer, was perhaps the first sign that the studio would go on to make arguably the definitive MMORPG.

While Kaplan and his colleague, Pat Nagle, initially designed World of Warcraft’s quest system to match EverQuest, player test feedback told them one thing: the game needed way more quests. Of the many ways WoW revolutionized the modern MMORPG, creating a seemingly never-ending quest chain that propelled players through the world’s regions is perhaps the most important, setting the mold for quest systems moving forward. There are over 10,000 unique quests, and even the most hardcore players still find themselves challenged with new daily and weekly activities delivered by patches and expansions.

In the modern live-service landscape, World of Warcraft’s approach to questing is increasingly niche. The idea of the never-ending hobby game has drifted away from the concept of living a second life in another world alongside hundreds of players, finding new ground in the likes of competitive shooters – a genre with little need for narrative rigour and a sense of adventure. That has brought with it a shift away from vast troves of unique quests, with many games instead prioritizing lightning play sessions buffeted by the ingenious corporate creation of the ‘Battle Pass’. Games like Call of Duty and Apex Legends offer simple challenges like ‘eliminate four players’ or ‘get five knockdowns’ for short-term XP buffs, allowing players to make their infinite grind slightly shorter to get ever-closer to that mythical level 90 skin. For these games, narrative is now occasional lore drops, event-driven cutscenes, and seasonal set dressing.

But while live-service is now dominated by very different types of games, the MMORPG still remains. It’s a less stable genre than it once was – Amazon’s lavish New World launched in 2021 and will close for good next year – but a new Guild Wars is on the horizon, and Final Fantasy 14 has been a huge success for Square Enix. The three titans of the MMO’s golden age – Ultima Online, EverQuest, and World of Warcraft – all continue to run to this day. In that sense, they have proven the ultimate live-service games, generating revenue for multiple decades.

Why these three have survived far beyond the genre’s mid-2000s heyday is thanks to the three key tenets that Long, Trost, and Kaplan have all followed: learn from what came before and find gaps to innovate within; build an engaging world that intrigues players and makes them want to take ownership of it; and above all else, look to fulfil those clear wishes of gamers that haven’t yet been realised. As Kaplan mentions, you can’t create greatness out of a vacuum: “You have to take inspiration. You have to try and evolve the art form and move it forward in some way. It’s not about the idea. It’s about the execution.”

The trio’s legacies have come from constant communication not just with their playerbases, but with one another, too. They are a model for the ideal live-service game: living and breathing, open to change, headed by custodians who aren’t afraid to push things forward whilst acknowledging their contemporaries. So why, despite their servers remaining live and new content being developed, does it feel like these games have disappeared? Well, MMO developers have granted a lot of wishes since 1996. Perhaps there’s nothing left to wish for.

“Now we’re getting pretty niche, and it’s harder to fulfil [those wishes] for audiences. We’re seeing it across film and TV as well as games”, Long says.

Technology has rapidly evolved and expanded, and with it, the cost of investment. “The table stakes required to even be considered by the gaming public are now so high it becomes difficult to justify the investment it takes”, Trost believes. When even Amazon can’t make the MMORPG work, it’s easy to see why bringing a new one to life is such a challenge.

Even if you have the financial backing to launch your bold new MMO, the question remains: will your audience have the attention span to invest into it? “The market overall has moved to much, much shorter play cycles over the last two decades,” Long explains. The average playtime for World of Warcraft ranges from 10 to 20 hours per week, with each individual session typically demanding a few hours of questing. Raiding takes even more time. While this overall time commitment can easily be met by a shooter’s most ardent fans, particularly in the era of the battle pass grind, there is a notable difference between the way each genre makes demands of a player’s attention. The modern live-service game has taken the essential bones of the MMORPG – those massive populations playing together – but has shifted its core away from a long-term communal hub to a quick ‘jump in, jump out’ combat spree.

That transformation has impacted the way a game’s population develops. “The ubiquitous nature of community doesn’t feel confined to the game anymore - it’s fragmented out across all our social media”, Trost notes. In an MMORPG, the community exists within a shared world. They can meet in a particular city, quest together in a specific region. This sense of being a genuine population living together in a digital reality creates a very different community than those grown on a game’s sub-reddit. Deep, meaningful connections were formed in World of Warcraft through the many hours that players sunk into its world every week – many real-life couples and even marriages have formed from the time taken planning raids together. And while the same has surely happened as a result of a fateful lobby match-up, it’s hard to imagine many Fortnite players finding that same connection when each match takes place in a confined battlefield and lasts just 15 to 20 minutes.

This shift in how multiplayer communities are grown and fostered is just a small part of a much larger change. Gaming is like travelling to a new holiday destination: it transports you to incredible, unknown lands and allows you to play out transient fantasies of a different life. In the early 2000s, games were the destination; World of Warcraft, EverQuest, and Ultima Online all offered a centralized hub that was an immersive world to explore. In 2026, games are no longer the destination – they’ve become the airport. Call of Duty’s menu is a departure list made up of rowdy weekend getaways. Fortnite is a portal to thousands of unique, custom islands hosting events powered by charting musicians and massive brands. And Roblox not only offers a plethora of worlds-upon-worlds to explore, but has formed an alluring ecosystem where players can not only craft those worlds themselves, but also be paid to do it. Everything from Grand Theft Auto and Call of Duty to Among Us and even Fortnite have been recreated in its virtual universe.

The Roblox community has evolved beyond players into mini development studios. These virtual worlds now belong to the players even more than the original developers themselves. During the era of the MMORPG, developers discovered that they were creating worlds for an autonomous population with wants and needs. Since then, player autonomy has rapidly evolved. It’s no longer about wondering when the next Warcraft expansion will come and continue the story. There’s a bustling embryonic mini gaming industry taking shape across these platforms, with a community that’s set to grow exponentially over the next five years. The real question, then, is can these platforms keep up? Because the era of live-service that came after MMORPGs suggests that’s a much, much harder task than simply designing a hit video game.

Sab Astley is a freelance writer who has written for IGN, Polygon, TotalFilm, Rolling Stone, Radio Times, and Metro UK.

articles.title: Best Buy Announces Midnight Opening for Ocarina of Time Launch, Zelda Switch 2 Consoles Also Up for Grabs
articles.summary: Best Buy is opening select stores at midnight on Nov. 5 for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launch day, featuring surprise restocks of the limited-edition Zelda 40th Anniversary Switch 2.
articles.body:
Best Buy has announced it will be opening select stores at midnight for the launch of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The major US retailer is gearing up for the highly anticipated release, with its website also now featuring a countdown to November 5.

The midnight launch will also include a fresh batch of stock for the limited-edition Zelda 40th Anniversary Nintendo Switch 2 consoles and matching Switch 2 Pro controllers.

That's potentially good news for anyone who missed out on the special-edition console during the preorder excitement in September .

For now, Best Buy hasn't specified how many systems will be available or which stores will receive stock, but it has warned that quantities are limited. Best Buy has also said that store hours will vary depending on region, so you'll want to check with your local store before heading out.

If you already have an Ocarina of Time preorder set for shipping and would prefer to collect it during the midnight opening, Best Buy has said you can also do this by modifying your order through your "Best Buy purchase history".

There is a good reason for fans to preorder elsewhere, however, as both Amazon and Walmart have Ocarina of Time listed for $59.88 instead of $69.99 .

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (Switch 2)

They will be available from October 29, but are currently sold out at every major retailer in the U.S .

Other highlights in the Nintendo Direct included the first gameplay reveal for Ocarina of Time , as well as a release date.

This is a full remake of the 1998 Nintendo 64 original game, with overhauled graphics that bring it up to modern standards.

According to Nintendo, this is a "faithful interpretation" for new hardware, but it does have a few more lines of dialogue for the characters you meet along the way, to give them more personality.

articles.title: ‘Mad Sandhu’ murder: How a Punjab Police tip-off led to accused’s arrest in Ahmedabad
articles.summary: Ahmedabad crime branch arrested Parminder Prasad alias Parminder Kaka for social media influencer Mad Sandhu’s Oct 3 Amritsar murder; to be handed to Punjab Police.
articles.body: AHMEDABAD: The city crime branch on Wednesday arrested a key accused in the murder of Punjab-based social media influencer ‘Mad Sandhu’. Based on an input shared by Amritsar police, the accused, Parminder Prasad alias Parminder Kaka, was traced to the city’s Vadaj area.He had allegedly fired at Sandhu and had arranged the motorcycle used in the murder, investigators said.Sandhu, also known as Madhusudan Sandhu, was shot dead on Oct 3 on Loharka Road in Amritsar. According to police, two men riding a motorcycle approached him when he had gone to collect his car from a service centre and opened fire before fleeing. Sandhu died on the way to the hospital.An FIR was registered at Amritsar’s Cantonment police station under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.A social media account associated with Goldy Dhillon allegedly claimed responsibility for the murder after the attack. Police are probing the suspected involvement of members of the gang in the killing.According to investigators, Parminder was the one who carried out the firing and arranged the motorcycle on which he arrived with the other assailant. After the murder, Parminder allegedly fled Punjab and reached Ahmedabad in an attempt to evade arrest.Crime branch officials said Amritsar Police shared information about Parminder’s involvement and his possible presence in Ahmedabad. “Parminder Prasad was fleeing to Mumbai and had broken his journey in Ahmedabad. He was arrested from Vadaj,” crime branch sources said.Officers are questioning Parminder to establish his movements after the murder, identify others involved in the killing and ascertain how he reached Ahmedabad. His mobile phone, travel details and contacts will also be examined.Police said he will be handed over to Punjab Police for further investigation and legal proceedings.The murder had drawn attention because Sandhu was a known social media personality, makeup artist and fashion designer. articles.title: Marvel Announces New Spy TV Series Zodiac, Coming in 2028
articles.summary: Marvel Studios has announced a brand new TV series called Zodiac, which will release in 2028.
articles.body:
Marvel Studios has announced a brand new TV series called Zodiac, which will release in 2028.

The show was officially announced at New York Comic Con, but was reported on last month. The Hollywood Reporter had mentioned it as a secondary piece of information when reporting on the cancellation of Daredevil: Born Again . Not much is known about the project other than it is a spy story that will seemingly center around Marvel's secretive government organization, SHIELD.

JUST ANNOUNCED AT NYCC: Marvel Television’s Zodiac is coming to Disney+ in 2028. — Marvel Studios (@MarvelStudios) October 8, 2026

JUST ANNOUNCED AT NYCC: Marvel Television’s Zodiac is coming to Disney+ in 2028.

Marvel has confirmed that it will begin casting the show in the next few weeks and the series will begin filming next year. The series, like other MCU shows, will premiere on Disney+. It's unclear exactly what the show will be about beyond the fact it's a spy thriller. We also have no idea which Marvel heroes will be in it. It wouldn't be surprising if Samuel L. Jackson's Nick Fury makes an appearance given his role within SHIELD. We can only hope that it's better than Secret Invasion, a series that Jackson led but was deemed to be a failure.

With the show releasing in 2028, it may also be set after Avengers: Secret Wars, which Jackson confirmed he will star in . The next two Avengers movies are expected to lay the ground work for a larger reset of the MCU , though Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige has denied that it will be a total reboot of the franchise.

articles.title: Resident Evil Requiem Was Originally Planned as an Online Game, Producer Says
articles.summary: Resident Evil Requiem producer Masachika Kawata revealed that the game was originally planned to be an online title before they scrapped the idea to focus on horror.
articles.body:
Resident Evil Requiem producer Masachika Kawata revealed that the game was originally planned to be an online title before they scrapped the idea to focus on horror.

Kawata shared this information in the Biohazard 30th Special Mook (‘magazine book’), a 124-page, full-color fan book with a complete history of the series' timeline, creature genealogy, and developer interviews.

“Every game is a continuous process of trial and error. For example, with Resident Evil Requiem, [game director Koshi Nakanishi] initially went so far as to develop it as an online game,” he said, via a fan translation.

“However, the results of research conducted partway through development were not favorable, so we decided to prioritize the horror concept once again and abandoned the online direction.”

That’s not the only wild thing Kawata revealed in the mook; he also said that Leon was the first character the team chose as a protagonist, but they ultimately felt that being able to hack and slash zombies with ease would lean too heavily on the "action" side of things, making the overall game less scary.

“Leon was also the first character confirmed to appear as a protagonist. However, we determined that with Leon alone, who excels in combat, ‘horror would no longer work,’ so it was decided to introduce Grace as a new character,” he continued.

Kawata also explained why Capcom decided to wait before sharing Leon’s involvement in the game, saying, “By keeping the full picture of the game, which would develop along both the horror and action sides, until the very end, we were able to successfully maintain interest in it up until release.”

Nakanishi’s early plans to make RE9 an online game isn’t something totally surprising, given that management at Capcom had also pushed for Resident Evil 7 to have multiplayer and microtransactions during its conceptual phase.

"Right around that time, there was a big push at Capcom, a big 'marketing' push, saying 'we have to make the games players are asking for,'" franchise producer Jun Takeuchi said in 2022. "So we were being told 'make this, make that', it was really hard on the directors at the time. 'Online multiplayer' this, 'downloadable content' that. 'Ongoing service games! Microtransactions! Make a Resident Evil game that ticks all those boxes!'

“The idea of multiplayer got killed off pretty quickly. If we could properly put it together, we could make an exciting horror multiplayer game, but we didn’t really have any good ideas, so we set it aside. We went down the list, chopping them out, until we had marketing’s worst nightmare — a regular old single-player horror game."

Capcom is moving full speed ahead with many of its high-profile IPs, Resident Evil being one of them. The series just enjoyed a film adaptation directed by Zach Cregger, and a Code Veronica remake is set to release in February next year. Given that the devs of RE9 didn’t move forward with an online version of the game, it’s possible that we see another online Resident Evil title in the future — perhaps another Resident Evil Outbreak?

articles.title: Smile 2 Star Kyle Gallner Wants to Play V in Paramount’s Cyberpunk 2077 Movie
articles.summary: Smile 2 star Kyle Gallner is making it known that he’s ready and willing to play V in Paramount’s film adaptation of Cyberpunk 2077.
articles.body:
Smile 2 star Kyle Gallner is making it known that he’s ready and willing to play V in Paramount’s live-action film adaptation of Cyberpunk 2077.

Cyberpunk 2077 has come a long way from its roots as a tabletop RPG. Thanks to CD Projekt Red’s video game and its standout expansion, as well as the critically-acclaimed Edgerunners spinoff anime from Studio Trigger, fans of the gritty sci-fi series are eating well.

They’re about to get fed even more, as Paramount revealed that it is developing a live-action movie based on the franchise. Thus far, we’re not sure of any plot details, so it’s possible that we could follow V’s adventures with Johnny Silverhand, or Idris Elba’s Solomon Reed before he meets V — or heck, maybe even Edgerunner 2’s Weak Kingsley, for all we know!

What we do know is that there’s no shortage of possibilities for this film, and that’s what has fans so excited. One of these fans is none other than actor Kyle Gallner, who is raring to step into Night City as the male version of V.

Mere hours after Paramount announced the news on October 8, Gallner posted a photo of himself sporting a close-shaved crop of hair, similar to V’s hairstyle in the game’s marketing materials, along with the caption: “Take me to night city.”

It’s safe to say that fans are pretty enthusiastic about this possible casting, with many already envisioning Gallner alongside Keanu Reeves’ Johnny Silverhand.

Take me to night city. — Kyle Gallner (@KyleGallner) October 8, 2026

“Kyle and Keanu. Sounds outstanding,” one wrote, while another said Gallner would be “PERFECT casting.”

“You and Keanu teaming up? I could be on board for that,” another commented.

“He’s HIM! Paramount, please consider,” yet another vouched.

For now, details about the movie are being kept under wraps, but CDPR co-CEO Michał Nowakowski promised that more information will come soon.

"We're excited about Paramount as a future partner who shares our creative ambitions for the Cyberpunk franchise," he said on X. "We look forward to sharing more details at the appropriate time."

While they wait for more news, fans can look forward to Edgerunners 2 , set to air on Netflix on October 20, 2026.

articles.title: Avatar: Seven Havens Premieres This Week — Here's When You Can Watch New Episodes
articles.body:
Avatar: Seven Havens premieres this week, introducing us to the first new Avatar in over 10 years. Original creators Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko returned for the 2D series, which follows a new Avatar, Pavi, over 200 years after The Legend of Korra. That’s around 300 years after the events of The Last Airbender.

Seven Havens will be streaming exclusively on Paramount+, now under the Skydance banner . The full series is slated for 26 half-hour episodes, just like the good ol’ days. However, those episodes will be split into two “Books,” the Avatar version of seasons.

Avatar: Seven Havens Book 1 Premieres This Week

The first three episodes of Book 1 will premiere on October 9. Subsequent episodes will be released in batches every Friday, so all 13 episodes of the Seven Havens will be streaming by the end of October.

As mentioned, the series will be streaming exclusively on Paramount+. Previous Avatar shows have eventually been released on DVD and Blu-ray, but that seems less likely for Seven Havens in the current Paramount era.

Episode titles were originally reported by Polygon , alongside promotional art for each batch:

Avatar: Seven Havens Episode Title Reveals

As for what to expect from the show, Seven Havens follows the usual Avatar tradition by picking up with, well, a new Avatar. The star of the new animated series is a young earthbender named Pavi.

Korra picked up less than a century after The Last Airbender, entering an era of industrialization in an otherwise recognizable version of the Four Nations. Seven Havens, in contrast, jumps over 200 years into the future.

Early trailers show an entirely distinct post-apocalyptic world that generally despises the notion of the Avatar. Given the amount of time that’s passed, it’s possible something happened to the Avatar Cycle to cause a delay in its continuation after Korra’s passing. Otherwise, Korra may have hit a Kyoshi-level lifespan.

Either way, it seems like some real crazy stuff went down after Korra and Asami walked into the sunset .

Paramount, which has completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. , has been rebuilding the Avatar franchise over the past couple of years. Most recently, Paramount dropped Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender, a new animated movie featuring the original Gaang all grown up. That was notoriously leaked online in protest of Paramount’s refusal to give it a theatrical release, but we were fans of the movie nonetheless.

Otherwise, while Seven Havens has already been greenlit for 26 episodes, there’s no word on when we’ll actually see Book 2. We’ll likely hear more about the series’ future as well as other projects like the Avatar fighting game at NYCC this weekend.

articles.title: Jay and Silent Bob’s Joint Venture Trailer and Game Details Revealed for Weed Farming Sim | NYCC 2026
articles.summary: Jay and Silent Bob’s Joint Venture turns Kevin Smith’s View Askewniverse into a foul-mouthed cozy weed farming simulator. New details and the first trailer were revealed at New York Comic Con 2026.
articles.body:
Nitrate Games revealed the first footage and new details about its upcoming farm sim video game Jay and Silent Bob’s Joint Venture at New York Comic Con on Thursday. IGN can exclusively share the first trailer for the game, which you can watch via the player embedded below.

Jay and Silent Bob’s Joint Venture promises a funny and raunchy spin on the cozy farming genre, with creator Kevin Smith’s iconic characters out to “build the best weed farm in town.” Players will build, cultivate and expand their operation, interact with familiar faces, and experience an original story written by Ernie Altbacker (the animated films Batman: Hush and Justice League Dark).

Kevin Smith and Jason Mewes have been creative forces on the project from the start.

“Since Jay and Silent Bob are the stars of this hilarious growing game, I cannot wait to play with myself!,” said Kevin Smith in a statement provided to IGN. “Many thanks to Nitrate Games for taking my little animals to this crossing and making them Stars Dew a Valley!”

“Joint Venture is a Jay and Silent Bob game, but it’s actually a continuation of Kevin Smith’s View Askewniverse,” says Nitrate Games co-founder Montana Sommese. “The central narrative picks up where the films left off, making the game a kind of sequel. Players can befriend and engage with their favorite characters from Kevin Smith's movies like never before. As we update the game over time, we're excited to be able to expand Kevin's story universe with narrative updates that will continue building from his cinematic universe.”

The NYCC panel revealed that other familiar faces from the View Askewniverse appear in the game, including Clerks’ Dante, Randal and Veronica; Mallrats’ Brodie and T.S. Quint; Chasing Amy’s Holden, Banky, Hooper and Alyssa; Dogma’s Azrael and Serendipity; Clerks II’s Becky & Elias; and Mooby.

Jay and Silent Bob’s Joint Venture is currently heading toward its play testing phase of production, with an expected release in late Spring 2027 on Steam/PC. A console release is also slated for 2027. Fans can learn more and s ign up to playtest and wishlist.
