articles.title: Charlie Cox on the Return of The Defenders — 'There Needed to Be Some Kind of Closure' | NYCC 2026
articles.summary: Charlie Cox is telling fans to "get the Save Daredevil Campaign" going as Daredevil: Born Again Season 3 will be the show's last.
articles.body:
Charlie Cox hit New York Comic Con today to join in the Marvel Television panel — jetlagged and just in from Dublin, but ready to talk the return of Daredevil for Season 3 of Born Again. And not just the return of the Horned One, but also his old teammates The Defenders.

"I think there needed to be a full circle with that story," Cox told IGN's Jeffrey Vega today after the panel. "There needed to be some kind of closure with it."

The Defenders of course originated in the Netflix Marvel era, where each character — Daredevil, Jessica Jones (Krysten Ritter), Luke Cage (Mike Colter), and Iron Fist (Finn Jones) — had their own series before teaming up for the 2017 Defenders season. Eventually those shows all came to an end, but when Cox and Vincent D'Onofrio showed up in the proper MCU, it seemed like only a matter of time before the street-level heroes would be reunited.

Charlie Cox, Finn Jones, and Krysten Ritter reunite on the #NYCC stage! #Daredevil — Marvel Studios (@MarvelStudios) October 8, 2026

Charlie Cox, Finn Jones, and Krysten Ritter reunite on the #NYCC stage! #Daredevil

"And Marvel were willing and able to bring them back and have a lot of fun with it," the actor said of the quartet returning. "It was great. We're such good friends. We have a great time together. There's some really interesting, fun dynamics that the fans seem to love, so it was great."

Part of that fun, Cox joked, was Mike Colter "giving away spoilers non-stop" — referring of course to the actor putting some info on social earlier this year that he shouldn't have. "We had to ban him from getting sides on set!"

As for whether or not Born Again Season 3, which has been confirmed to be the last season of the show, means we won't see Cox put on the horns again, the actor says it might be up to the fans to decide on that front.

"Don't know, man. I don't know," he said when asked whether or not he's done as Daredevil. "I mean, it might be. It might be. Don't worry about Kevin [Feige]. Get the Save Daredevil campaign on the horn. Get them motivated. That engine, that won't stop until there's some resolution. That's my true superpower -- is the Save Daredevil campaign!"

Talk to Scott Collura @scottcollura.bsky.social , or listen to his Star Trek podcast, Transporter Room 3 . Or do both!

Jeffrey Vega is the Lead Social Host/Producer at IGN and is probably feeding his neopets right now. You can follow him on Twitter @jeffreyvega , Instagram , and IGN's TikTok .

articles.title: Jessica Chastain's Other Mommy Is a Horror Film That Never Figures Out Its Own Identity
articles.summary: Review: Jessica Chastain’s Other Mommy is a great idea looking for a better movie.
articles.body:
Although she’s made her reputation (and her Academy Award) on prestige dramas, Jessica Chastain is no stranger to horror. The Sacramento-born thespian has starred in the likes of Mama, It: Chapter Two, and the underrated Guillermo del Toro joint Crimson Peak, and once more returns to the genre with Other Mommy , a new film from director Rob Savage where Chastain plays the dual role of a mother and her demonic doppelganger. Sadly, the film wastes what should be a slam dunk premise (and a trailer that went viral based on a well-timed jump scare) on a generic script and not enough ideas to fill out even its brisk 90-minute runtime.

Arabella Olivia Clark stars as Bela, a seven-year-old girl living a not-quite idyllic suburban family life with distant mother Ursula (Chastain) and doting father Russell (Jay Duplass). There’s some tension in the home stemming from Ursula’s seeming workaholic lifestyle that Bela is already aware is actually a cover for her mother having an affair, but not enough that her parents haven’t been blissfully unaware that Bela has been hanging out with a not-imaginary friend named Other Mommy (also Chastain). Other Mommy loves spending time with Bela when Ursula can’t be bothered but also won’t stop insisting that Bela agree to let Other Mommy “into her heart,” the outcome of which is assuredly some form of demonic possession but also isn’t explained enough for the audience to dread it.

What follows is a surprisingly quick acknowledgment from Ursula and Russell that something supernatural is going on, and the family fleeing their home to locale after locale where Other Mommy inevitably arrives to cause more mystic mayhem. In a strange move for a movie like this, Savage rarely tries to mine fear from the setting or its corruption thereof, instead betting all his chips on how Other Mommy distorts herself and the scene around her with reality-warping powers that can’t help but come off like hollow, budget-conscious spectacle. The inconsistency in how Other Mommy’s sinister illusions manifest removes a lot of their bite; one scene features an extended shot of Chastain’s neck stretching with unconvincing CGI, while another features some agreeably gooey practical body horror that’s shown for only a few seconds. This approach results in a movie that doesn’t come close to being as unnerving as it clearly wants to be.

Not helping matters is the impression that the movie can’t settle on a coherent identity, instead grabbing bits and pieces from other movies and trying them on for size like Other Mommy does with other people’s skins. Savage invokes movies like It, Smile, Coraline, and The Conjuring (that last one is understandable given James Wan’s producer credit here), but never delivers an iconic visual or concept that other movies could hypothetically crib from him. Even the main conceit of Chastain playing the dual lead role is watered down by Other Mommy sometimes taking on different disguises, a confounding gambit given that the movie never tries to generate suspense from the characters possibly not knowing who in the room is Other Mommy. It all leads to a conclusion centered around revealing the dark family secret that made Other Mommy target Bela in the first place, but the answer is too little too late to make the journey worth the effort.

Still, the reason to see this is why anyone will bother picking up a ticket: Jessica Chastain breaking bad as Other Mommy. Chastain taking her bread and butter intensity and channeling it into a maternal Deadite is the kind of hook that will likely catapult Other Mommy to profitability regardless of critical reviews. If only Savage was more willing to trust his leading lady, often smothering Chastain’s incredible physical performance with droopy facial VFX and rapid cuts. Nathan Elston's screenplay also never gives her a character to play on the other side of the coin, with Ursula being more of a checklist of “unattentive mother” tropes instead of a human being. There’s no exploration of Ursula’s emotional reality and why she can only seem to care for Bela in an ancillary capacity to make effective contrast with Other Mommy’s malicious clinginess. If Ursula doesn’t want to be part of the family, what does she want? The movie doesn’t seem to know.

Chastain still commits even with such flimsy material, and to give Savage credit, he does a great job directing Arabella Olivia Clark to a child performance that’s one of the best parts of the movie. Bela has more screen time than anyone else, and the movie avoids many of the pitfalls of having a child lead even when the storytelling often comes up short in other ways. The most specificity that the family unit gets is everyone referring to Russell as “Daddo” instead of “Daddy” – a cute detail that wouldn’t be remarkable if the movie didn’t have an emotional vacancy where its dramatic engine should be. Even the gore and scare sequences don't leave much impact beyond a couple of early exceptions, resulting in a film that unfortunately runs out of energy long before the credits roll.

articles.title: Finn Jones Calls Iron Fist’s Return in Daredevil: Born Again a 'Wonderful Gift' | NYCC 2026
articles.summary: Finn Jones addresses his return as Danny Rand/Iron Fist in Daredevil: Born Again Season 3, calling a second chance with Marvel a 'wonderful gift.'
articles.body:
Speaking with IGN at New York Comic Con 2026 , Iron Fist actor Finn Jones calls his return to the MCU as Danny Rand in Daredevil: Born Again Season 3 “a wonderful gift” and shed light on how his character has “evolved” since The Defenders .

“It's wild to not play a character for 10 years and then come back after all that time. For an actor, it's a wonderful gift,” Jones told us following the Marvel Television panel . “I think personally people grow a lot in 10 years and as an actor you grow a lot and characters grow a lot as well. So to come back with all of that kind of story and to bring that forward into this what I see is it's kind of like a new version of Danny Rand or a more of an evolved, grownup version is really fun. So fun.”

While Jones couldn’t reveal too much about what happens with Danny in the upcoming third and final season of Daredevil: Born Again , he told us how he imagined his own backstory of what the character has been up to in the many years since he was last seen.

“I think he's been around the world uh in various different secret orders, probably a lot of like down in ancient ruins in South America and in Asia and really honing his craft,” says Jones. “I think he's gone through a lot of grief and a lot of joy and I think that's really forged the Danny that we see show up in Daredevil Season 3. That's all my own backstory. That's just that's just like where I believe the character has been and then what we see in the show is I think a culmination of that.”

Jones calls the Danny Rand in Daredevil: Born Again “very, very grounded” and with “a different quality to him, which is just a joy to play.”

Jones also recalled what it was like to step back on set opposite his fellow Defenders co-stars Charlie Cox (Daredevil), Krysten Ritter (Jessica Jones) and Mike Colter (Luke Cage).

Marvel Cinematic Universe: Every Upcoming Movie and TV Show

“It was so charged, you know, like a lot of anticipation and so there was definitely nerves, but there was also a lot of excitement. And I think when you're in that kind of environment, it allows you to really sharpen and focus [on] what you want to bring. And so, it just felt very dynamic,” says Jones. “Being with these guys again – with Charlie and Krysten and Mike – there's such a great chemistry between all four of us that you can really just relax into the dynamic that's just between us all.”

“The way that they've written Danny this year is – I'm just so grateful. I'm just so grateful [for] the level of attention that's been put into the character. And I remember getting the scripts and I was just like, ‘I got no notes.’ I'm just ready to show up and give my all.

Jones adds, “And I have to say the stunt team working with [coordinator] Phil Silvera and his team have been really they're they're the best. They are the best and I'm so grateful to have them be so supportive and so imaginative bringing Danny Rand back into the MCU.”

Daredevil: Born Again returns for its final season in 2027.

articles.title: Singing `New York, New York,' Rays revel in recognition as they head to AL Championship Series
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Belting out “Theme from New York, New York” as they locked arms in the visitors' clubhouse at Yankee Stadium, the Tampa Bay Rays reveled with...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Belting out "Theme from New York, New York" as they locked arms in the visitors' clubhouse at Yankee Stadium, the Tampa Bay Rays reveled with satisfaction after sweeping baseball's most storied team.

"The best team in the world right here," Tampa Bay star Junior Caminero said Wednesday night after the Rays earned a matchup with the Chicago White Sox or Cleveland Guardians in their first American League Championship Series since 2020.

Fresh off a three-game sweep of the Yankees in their Division Series, the Rays on Monday will host an ALCS game at Tropicana Field for the first time since 2008 — their 2020 seven-game win over Houston was played at San Diego's Petco Park because of the coronavirus pandemic.

"I love popping bottles," said Ryan Vilade, a 27-year-old journeyman who played his first game since Sept. 27 in the Game 3 clincher against New York. "I love drinking beer and I love popping bottles."

Vilade and Victor Mesa Jr. homered in Tampa Bay's 4-3 victory Wednesday night. During the celebration, Caminero mimicked late Yankees broadcaster John Sterling, yelling: "Theeee Yankees lose!"

"We got two more bites — two more bites on the bone!" manager Kevin Cash screamed. "Nobody sleeps!"

Tampa Bay finished an AL-best 98-64 in the regular season, then dominated the Yankees to reach its third ALCS and remain on track for a possible first World Series title.

"We'll enjoy it and we'll have a little time here to organize ourselves," president of baseball operations Erik Neander said. "When you've got five starters throwing the way these do, it makes it a little easier not to overthink it too much."

Tampa Bay was just behind Milwaukee for the top regular-season team batting average, .2585 to .2581, and led the AL in on-base percentage. The Rays were second in the AL with a .296 batting average on balls in play.

"The identity of our team, that's kind of the versatility that we have," outfielder Jonny DeLuca said. "A lot of our guys are quick and fast in putting the ball in play, and I think in playoffs it makes a huge difference, whether it's getting down the line, baserunning, defense, whatever it is. I think the speed is a huge aspect to our game, and, yeah, it's helped us a lot."

Cash, who led his team to the postseason for the sixth time in eight years, arrived in the interview room Wednesday night relatively dry.

"This is my second shirt, second hat. I've changed it twice," he said. "Cami just sprayed something on me and so did Victor. Both of them did. I said, `This is a dry shirt.' If they want to play the next game, they'll stop."

After a 2025 season spent playing across the bay in Tampa, Florida, at the Yankees' spring training home, Steinbrenner Field, while Tropicana Field was repaired following damage caused by Hurricane Milton , the Rays returned this year to the Trop in St. Petersburg and drew 1.4 million fans.

After drawing a regular season-high crowd of 28,055, Tampa Bay removed tarps covering upper-deck seats and saw 40,452 fill the ballpark for Game 1 against the Yankees, their largest home crowd since Game 5 of the 2010 AL Division Series.

"Even from the intros, before the game, you could tell the turnout for the Rays fans was there, and we could feel that the whole day," said closer Bryan Baker, who saved all three ALDS games.

Tampa Bay drew 40,226 for Game 2 and expects a similar atmosphere for the ALCS.

Tampa Bay was 4-2 this year against the White Sox and 5-1 vs. Cleveland.

Going into the ALCS, the Rays will have played just three games in two weeks. Cash, however, didn't fear rust caused by earning the top AL seed and a first-round bye.

"The alternative is playing three must-win games or two out of three," he said in late September. "I'll take where we're at."

articles.title: How War Season 1, Episode 2 Escalates Dominic West and Sienna Miller’s High-Stakes Marital Battle Through Ruthless Legal Moves
articles.summary: This week’s episode is another well-acted, well-written affair. HBO’s War tightens the screws just enough in its second episode to brace viewers for either side of this divorce to mess things up beyond repair for their respective clients.
articles.body:
Full spoilers follow for War: Season 1 , Episode 2.

After a heavy dose of frenetic table-setting in the series premiere , War’s second episode — sharply written by George Kay and deftly directed by Ben Taylor — slows its pacing down a bit as Morgan (Dominic West) and Carla (Sienna Miller) and their respective legal teams enter the pivotal three-day mediation period of their divorce.

Morgan and Carla are each instructed by their teams to put on amicable fronts as both sides strategize how to strike the best deal. That means a lot of strained smiles and literal hand-holding between the divorcing spouses to mask any anger and bitterness. Their facades just barely hold. Behind the scenes, their teams are reckoning how to protect their clients and gain the upper hand.

After Carla was surprised on the red carpet with divorce papers, her lawyers at Taylor & Byrne want to control the developing narrative, namely the matter of Flora Monroe (Rose Williams), the young actress Carla enlisted to honey-trap Morgan in a one night stand.

Taylor & Byrne partner Serena (Phoebe Fox) tries to convince Flora to sign an NDA as a means to protect herself and Carla, but Flora is unnerved by the request. She’s not fond of being paid off as if she were a prostitute. Flora insists she chose to sleep with Morgan because she found him attractive.

Serena’s plan ends up backfiring spectacularly because her new hire, Johnny (Archie Renaux), is secretly on his first assignment as the mole for Morgan’s lawyers at Cathcarts. Johnny is funneling information to both firms about Serena’s offer to compensate Flora and detailing the shakedown engineered by Flora’s greedy mother Mumsy (a scene-stealing Camille Coduri). Needless to say, things are getting messy and murky for everyone as both legal teams play dirty.

Then there’s the curious implication that Johnny is growing romantically (or just sexually) interested in Carla and/or Flora. He hasn’t outright said anything but his search history and longing looks don’t lie. Johnny seems poised to not only screw up his relationship with his girlfriend Bella (Honor Swinton Byrne) but the entire divorce case for both firms.

Flora also seems ready to make things even worse for herself by texting Morgan in the episode’s closing moments. Is she playing her own separate angle or does she legitimately want to be with Morgan romantically again? We shall see.

West and Miller excel in this episode at smiling through their teeth at each other, while Renaux continues to find the humanizing nuances in the double-dealing Johnny. Fox’s Serena seems like the closest thing to a good guy in this story, but there’s enough iffy moral resolve in her that maybe she will end up surprising viewers with an eventual turn to the dark side.

As Serena’s adversaries Beatrice “Queen Bea” Ubosi and St John Smallwood, respectively, Nina Sosanya and Pip Torrens continue to be a great one-two punch duo who find enough wit and aplomb in their predatory characters to put the guilty in guilty pleasure.

articles.title: Creators Robert and Michelle King Deliver a Sly Smart Look at Silicon Valley With the New Series Cupertino
articles.summary: Cupertino Season 1 premiere review: The Good Wife creators Robert and Michelle King are back with a sly, smart deconstruction of Silicon Valley.
articles.body:
Full spoilers follow for the season premiere of CBS' Cupertino .

The world is a little bit easier to take when there’s a topical drama by Robert and Michelle King on our televisions. From thorny legal battles (The Good Wife, The Good Fight) to religious conundrums (Evil), the Kings have tackled some of the more complex issues in modern life with humor, pathos, and realism. Gratefully, they’re back to help us parse the current tsunami of tech threats from pervasive AI to infringed privacy with Cupertino.

"Michael & Olivia" opens with Silicon Valley lawyers Michael Price (Mike Colter) and Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller) separately getting unceremoniously canned by their tech start-up employer, S-Talk. Michael is an equity co-founder, while Olivia is a junior lawyer one year out of law school, but getting career-dumped is today’s great equalizer. As they awkwardly commiserate on the curb and share some genuine admiration for one another’s work, Olivia throws him an information bone because he’s always been nice to her. While working with owner Richard Everett (Will Brill), she heard him asking someone how to fire an equity partner for cause while keeping their money… meaning Michael was unlawfully pushed out.

From that little moment of allegiance blooms the duo who are the beating heart of Cupertino. Colter’s been a ride-or-die actor for the Kings going back to The Good Wife, and here he brings smarts, charisma, and simmering sex appeal to Michael Price. Though this character wears tailored suits and comes from a prestigious family of lawyers, Michael is a believer in the Davids battling these tech Goliaths, which keeps him grounded and empathetic. The yin to his yang is Rachel Keller’s Olivia, who is shrewd yet green. Post law school, she migrated straight to Silicon Valley from the sheltered arms of her rural Christian family, so there’s plenty for her to navigate as she starts swimming with the sharks. Fresh from the series Tokyo Vice , Keller was also stellar in FX’s Legion, so it's exciting to see her go toe-to-toe with not only Colter but Cupertino’s ever-expanding ensemble of top-notch recurring actors to come, including Girls5eva alums Busy Philipps and Renée Elise Goldsberry, Joe Morton, and Jackie Earle Haley.

If you’re an existing fan of the Kings’ work, Cupertino feels a little like comfort television because it utilizes many of their signature storytelling elements: ripped-from-the-headline cases; the casting of theater-great character actors; storylines that breathlessly twist on a dime; and their ability to make serious subjects comprehensible, weird, and entertaining. They’ve even 2.0’d their The Good Fight lady fixer character Marissa Gold, updating her as Michael and Olivia’s Gen Z street-smart office manager, Christy Palladino (Ella Stiller).

Yet familiar doesn’t mean this is a dumbed-down procedural by any means. The Cupertino pilot alone tackles tech industry sexual harassment and equity disparity, stealing personhood for LLMs, and the fragility of tech bros with their shell games and unethical smoke screens. It’s all presented with wit and intelligence, and through characters who bring us into this alien world of stealth technology and can decipher this industry that's moving too fast and breaking things with seeming impunity. Cupertino reminds us that there’s no shame in being a broadcast procedural when you’re working at the level of the Kings and their collaborators.

If The Good Wife and The Good Fight could give me an understanding of Constitutional law and systemic governmental flaws, I can’t wait to see what the Kings school me on with Cupertino.

articles.title: The Best LEGO Star Wars Sets to Build in 2026
articles.summary: Some of the best sets in the galaxy.
articles.body:
For over two decades, the LEGO and Star Wars partnership has endured and thrived. It is nothing if not consistent; the sets are geared toward every skill level, from beginner to advanced, and all of the sets – even the most rudimentary – are reliably high-quality. The massive ship and droid replicas get the most press. But even the more idiosyncratic sets – like the Gingerbread AT-AT, for example – still capture the look, feel, and whimsy of their inspirations.

TL;DR: These Are the Best Star Wars LEGO Sets

LEGO Jango Fett's Firespray-Class Starship

LEGO Jabba's Sail Barge – Collectors' Edition

LEGO Millennium Falcon (Collector's Edition)

LEGO is a costly hobby – one that requires a selective eye, so that only la crème de la crème makes it on your shopping list. Here, as of October 2026, are the Best LEGO Star Wars sets that you can buy. You can also check out our broader list of LEGO Technic sets for more STEM-focused options or dive into our picks for the best Star Wars gifts to buy right now.

This was the new LEGO Star Wars sets for 2025's May the Fourth . The largest iteration of Jango Fett's Starship to date, this vessel (better known to Star Wars diehards as Slave I), can be posed either in its landing mode or its flight mode. It comes with two minifigures of Jango Fett and young Boba Fett and possesses articulable blaster cannons.

This depiction of The Mandalorian's Grogu is not an exact duplicate of the show's depiction; rather, it's been exaggerated for maximum cuteness and presentability. The arms and head move, and the arms rotate via dials on the figure's back. The Hover Pram, Grogu's high-tech space bassinet, is mounted on a square black stand and completes the overall package.

A complementing, proportionally sized companion to the X-Wing Starfighter (#75355), this TIE Interceptor featured in Return of the Jedi as a defender of the second Death Star. We built this set at its launch, and it is currently available exclusively through the LEGO Store .

Jabba's Sail Barge (Collectors' Edition)

Jabba the Hutt is the slimiest, greediest gangster in the Dune Sea, and this Sailing Barge , which transports him and his cronies, is appropriately massive. It includes a full kitchen, an armory, and a prison cell for any disobedient servants. The set also comes with a Princess Leia minifigure in her slave costume, so you can recreate the iconic death scene from Return of the Jedi.

LEGO sets usually have a short production lifespan; the old sets get retired to make way for new ones. But the massive Millennium Falcon, which weighs in at 7541 pieces and launched in 2017, is still going strong. It's constantly on backorder, and for good reason; it's a modern classic amongst the LEGO faithful. It comes with two crews – the original crew, with Han, Luke, and Leia, and the sequel crew, with old Han Solo, Rey, and Finn. And it's got fully realized interiors in addition to its articulable exterior.

In 2017, back when this set launched, adult sets were the exception and not the rule. This was a groundbreaking testament to what LEGO could be. Today, with so many other sets that reach its level of complexity, it's a fulfilled example of what LEGO has become and one of the most expensive LEGO sets you can buy.

First introduced in Return of the Jedi, the AT-ST has a distinctive, two-legged appearance, which made them memorable adversaries for the underdog Ewoks, who used logs, slings, and arrows to take them down. This model is rotatable and posable, and its top opens to reveal a two-person cockpit.

Shockingly, the best LEGO Star Wars set out now is not the 9000+ piece Death Star . Instead, it's this Gingerbread AT-AT, which comes with a miniature gingerbread Darth Vader. If you're buying for a Star Wars lover this holiday season, you can't go wrong with this adorable build, which has Christmas lights on its chassis, candy canes for its turrets, and sugar icing on its edges. Plus, the price is right. We built, photographed, and reviewed this set , and we can't recommend it enough.

It might not cut as impressive a figure as its older, bigger brother from seven years ago, but this version of the Imperial Star Destroyer does have several advantages. It's more portable for one, which makes easier to incorporate into one's home decor. It comes with seven minifigures, including one of Cal Kestis from the Fallen Order and Survivor video games. And lastly, unlike the prior Destroyer, which was only a shell of a starship, this model opens up to reveal a bridge, command room, break room, and armory.

Fun and whimsical, this massive Darth Vader minifigure is scaled up to six times the size of a regular LEGO minifigure. It includes a large fabric cape and a red lightsaber that Vader can hold at different angles in his right hand.

Inspired by Season 1 of The Mandalorian, this set includes the Jawas and Sandcrawler that stripped The Razorcrest for spare parts, plus the Mudhorn that nearly killed Mando (until Grogu levitated the beast with the Force). The sandcrawler is well-detailed, with side panels that open to reveal the interior and dials that turn to open the front hatch and control the steering.

Standing nearly a foot-and-a half tall, this recreation of feared bounty hunter Boba Fett is poseable and comes with a fabric cape and a jet pack. It's the thematic equivalent to the LEGO Chewbacca that we built in 2024 , but with even more variance and theatricality.

This model of Darth Vader's flagship, appropriately shaped like a dagger, is an intimidating, monstrous build. The LEGO Star Wars brand has always been the record-breaker; its sets have the highest piece counts and the highest prices. And now, thanks to the LEGO Executor Super Star Destroyer, the brand has the longest set, beating out the LEGO Titanic by half an inch. It's a lot of grey-on-grey-grey, but it still has an interesting, varied look, thanks to the "greebling" that covers its surface.

There have been a lot of Star Wars LEGO sets over the years, and more and more new options arrive every year. As of October 2026, 74 LEGO Star Wars sets are available at the LEGO store, with options from pretty much every movie and show in the series.

Lots of times, when LEGO creates a set, it is an uncanny approximation of something real. The artistry is in making these bricks, rods, pins, and gears fit together and do something that perhaps, they weren't originally meant to do. But when it comes to Star Wars LEGO sets – especially the more massive ones – the vehicles and droids look unusually "native" – as if LEGO itself was conceived with Star Wars in mind. It's why the 4784-piece Imperial Star Destroyer looks more like a genuine Star Destroyer rather than a "LEGO" Star Destroyer.

This is part auspiciousness; the Star Wars universe is very angular, with clean lines that lend themselves to the LEGO aesthetic, And this also part effort; the designers put an outsized amount of time into "greebling" – the attention to micro surface detail that makes a monochromatic surface look layered, technically functional and interesting.

LEGO Star Wars sets, in other words, are in a class of their own.

Looking for more LEGO builds? Check out our roundup of the best LEGO Disney sets and the best LEGO Batman sets .

Kevin Wong is a contributing freelancer for IGN, specializing in LEGO. He's also been published in Complex, Engadget, Gamespot, Kotaku, and more. Follow him on Twitter at @kevinjameswong .

articles.title: Silver Pines Is the Silent Hill Metroidvania Mash-Up I Never Knew I Needed
articles.summary: Silver Pines Is the Silent Hill Metroidvania Mash-Up I Never Knew I Needed
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Tristan Ogilvie, who plays survival horror games like it's his job (because a lot of the time, it very much is).

While there’s certainly been a number of horror-themed metroidvanias released in recent years, from the savage executions of the Blasphemous series to the brilliant shapeshifting reverse-horror of Carrion, until now I’ve never experienced one that has so expertly adapted proper survival horror mechanics into the genre. Silver Pines takes the fear and foreboding of Silent Hill and Resident Evil, and flattens it into a 2.5D setting that begins as a small town but becomes an increasingly larger one as new tools are uncovered and new paths are unlocked in typical metroidvania fashion. I’m only about five hours into what is apparently a 12-hour story, but ever since I picked up this mystery-soaked adventure I’ve found it harder to put down than a family pet.

I’m admittedly a fairly easy mark here given that survival horror and metroidvanias are two of my personal favourite genres. It’s not a total shock to discover that I enjoy them when paired together. I also like beer and burgers, never more so than when I’m gripping one in each hand. However, taking the restricted inventory management and intentionally clumsy combat of classic survival horror and splicing them together with the sidescrolling viewpoint and exploration of a 2.5D metroidvania could easily have resulted in a mutation uglier than anything that’s ever emerged from an Umbrella Corporation lab. In the capable hands of developer Wych Elm Games, though, this unlikely coupling has turned out to be every bit as energising as the result of combining a green herb with a red one.

Just because its presentation has been crushed down into a 2.5D plane doesn’t mean that Silver Pines’ survival horror has sacrificed any of its gameplay depth. Boss fights are present and accounted for, right down to the panic induced by emptying your pockets of ammo reserves and never really knowing how close you have an enemy to death. You can’t get from one floor of a building to the next without solving elaborate strings of puzzles, like the repair of broken-down machinery and the correct alignment of combination locks. Then there’s the healthy variety of enemy types to contend with as you explore, from ghouls that pursue you menacingly on all-fours to Hitchcockian hordes of crows that swarm down from the trees, along with a slowly expanding arsenal of shotguns and rifles to combat them with.

Meanwhile Silver Pines’ slowly expanding suite of exploration tools doesn’t rely on typical powered-up double-jumps and unlockable grappling hooks in order to open up new paths to explore. Rather, it’s grounded in a way that feels far more appropriate to the Anytown, USA setting. The box cutter you just picked up in an office can be wielded as a melee weapon, but it can also be used to slash through the plastic sheets masking construction areas, opening up new rooms to ransack for clues to the whereabouts of Eddie Velvet, the missing singer you’re in search of. The sledgehammer can crush through weakened sections of concrete walls, the sewer key can lift manholes and access the surprisingly expansive tunnels below street level, and the pistol can be used to shoot padlocks off gates or the coverings from air vents to scramble up into.

Everything just feels so well thought out, right down to manually punching in numbers on the metallic keypads of the payphones dotted around the map in order to save your game. Sure, a similar mechanic was used in Silent Hill: Townfall just last month, but Silver Pines takes it a step further by demanding you actually feed in one of your precious few coins in order to make a call, money that could otherwise be used to purchase vital medkits or ammo from a vending machine. If you’re fresh out, you can even rummage around in the coin return slot for some uncollected spare change.

I also love how deliberate every action is in Silver Pines. From slowly chambering each individual round in your revolver while trying not to panic at the shadowy stalkers stumbling towards you, to pausing to wait for a pot of coffee to percolate in a police station break room in order to gulp down a piping hot increase to your stamina bar, almost everything you do in Silver Pines feels methodical. Silver Pines isn’t ever afraid to take that extra bit of time, whether it’s to painfully prolong the seconds of pure panic or to allow a rare moment of peace to be properly savoured.

In fact, at times I’ve gone beyond merely slowing down in Silver Pines; I’ve actually stopped completely and left the main character idling just to take a moment to absorb the incredible amount of atmosphere that’s been soaked into every frame. It may be viewed at a distance rather than over your character’s shoulder or in first-person, but Silver Pines still manages to draw you into its gloomy ghost town with an ominous ambience that’s every bit as engrossing as the most large-budgeted of survival horror standouts. It even has in-game serials that run on the televisions you pass in motel rooms and abandoned apartments, much like Alan Wake. The fact that this is the debut release for Wych Elm Games, apparently with a core development team of just five people, is honestly pretty remarkable.

As I said at the top, I’ve still got a long way to go with my investigation into Silver Pines so it’s too soon to pass judgment on it. However, if it manages to keep building on its incredible opening hours, then Silver Pines could well turn out to be one of my favourite games of 2026 – and that’s saying something in a year of gaming that’s arguably produced more must-play gems than any other in this console generation.

Now the only thing we need is a catchy portmanteau for what I hope becomes a well-populated new subgenre of metroidvanias. Er… Survivalvania? Look it’s not great, but it will have to do for now.

Silver Pines is available now on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, PC, Nintendo Switch, and Nintendo Switch 2.

Tristan Ogilvie is a senior video editor at IGN based in Sydney, Australia. He has 25 years of experience covering video games, having served as Deputy Editor on Official PlayStation 2 Magazine Australia and as Editor of Official Xbox 360 Magazine Australia, before joining IGN in 2009. You can find him on Bluesky @tristanogilvie.bsky.social

articles.title: Avatar: Seven Havens Bends It Like Pavi and Nisha in the First 3 Episodes of the Latest Installment in the Franchise
articles.summary: Avatar: Seven Havens episodes 1-3 recap and review: Twins take on the challenge of a post-apocalyptic world.
articles.body:
This review contains full spoilers for Avatar: Seven Havens Season 1, Episodes 1-3, which debut October 9 on Paramount+.

The experience of watching the first new Avatar series in 12 years — Avatar Aang movie and Netflix’s live-action adaptation aside — is an overwhelming one. While there have been numerous (pretty excellent) comic book tie-ins and extensions released in the intervening decade plus, insuring that the world created by Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko has never fully gone away, they’ve all felt like mere footsteps from the stellar runs of Avatar: The Last Airbender and The Legend of Korra — reinterpretations of information we already had on hand instead of something really truly new.

Avatar: Seven Havens, on the other hand, is really truly new. Set 225 years after the events of Legend of Korra in a post-apocalyptic landscape where all that remains of humanity is based in the Seven Havens of the title, the show evolves the animation style and setting in a way that’s closer to Miyazaki or recent surreal hits like Scavengers Reign or Common Side Effects rather than what we might expect from an Avatar series.

But even with the different animation, there’s something both alien and familiar about watching Seven Havens. On one hand, you’ve got a kid Avatar in Pavi (Saheli Khan) — more on that in a second — just like Aang in the original series. But unlike Aang, who had a very clear path forward (stop the Fire Lord, save the world), Pavi has been living on the outskirts with only bugs, rocks, and her cat-monkey (voiced by Dee Bradley Baker, the voice of Appa and Momo in the original series) as friends, with no clear path to saving a world that maybe doesn’t want to be saved.

The sly humor that DiMartino and Konietzko have woven into previous series is back, and an early sequence in the premiere, “On The Horizon,” with Jae (Major Curda) surfing his way through the Haven of Ellora is an utter delight. But if Korra took the franchise in darker, more adult directions, Seven Havens is both a reflection of the world we live in today and of the anger some fans felt toward the character of Korra. The plot involves something Korra did two centuries earlier that broke the world, leading to the survivors hating and fearing the Avatar; it’s also clear in the first three episodes that this story isn’t done, and it also isn’t what the world thinks. It’s just speculation, but it very much feels like DiMartino and Konietzko are saying, “Oh, you hate Korra so much? Well, here’s why you’re wrong , and we’ll lay it out for you over the course of 26 episodes.”

That aspect could be a little (well, a lot ) navel-gazing, but there’s the outward focus the creators are bringing to the story as well, diving harshly into both the divided nature of our own real world and the coming climate apocalypse. Animation is never going to have the pace necessary to really reflect the world outside our window — it usually takes at least two years for an animated season to make it from script to screen, unless you’re South Park — but thanks to an Avatar classic (a play at a festival performed by children), we discover why the world hates the monster Korra and how the Seven Havens were formed together but now stand far apart. In the third episode, “The Order,” the airbender Karthik (Akshay Khanna) — now promoted to Commander of the Bending Brigade in Ellora — suggests they reach out to the other Havens as fewer and fewer benders are being born every year. He’s flatly turned down: Ellora can stand for itself.

This isolationist stance has been bubbling over in our real world for a long time now, and it’s hard not to watch scenes like that without thinking about Brexit or America’s increasing push to close its borders. Similarly, the threats in the first few episodes — other than a menacing red diamond; more on that in a second — are all climate based. A tornado is the “villain” of the premiere, and a massive green storm nearly destroys Ellora in Episode 2, “Into The Storm.” Again, it’s not one to one, but with our own climate disasters increasing year by year, it’s clear that DiMartino and Konietzko are setting up Seven Havens as both a commentary and a warning, while also delivering a fun mythology-building Avatar series.

Speaking of mythology-building, the first two episodes essentially function like one pilot, and are surprisingly sparse on action and plot… laudably so, as the series in those initial 40ish minutes sits in the silences and lets us feel what the characters are feeling instead of thrill at Cool Bending Fights, though there are plenty of those too. The two plot tracks follow Pavi as she rides her cat-monkey, trying to hide while a festival celebrating the rise of the Seven Havens takes over Ellora; and Jae as he works with his bending team from the town’s Bending Brigade to help fix a crumbling bridge.

Pavi is, per the title of “Book 1,” all about survival and that’s it. Jae also ties into that theme; he’s focused on protecting Ellora to a fault, though having been raised in a post-Avatar society, he doesn’t seem to understand what he’s protecting or why. When Pavi ends up accidentally causing havoc at the festival by freeing some bugs, she uses her earthbending and alerts Jae to a rogue bender. Traveling out into a storm, Jae appeals to Pavi with kindness, but they get interrupted by a tornado, which Pavi helps shut down by revealing she can also airbend. This reshapes Jae’s whole thinking: What if the Avatar isn’t a monster, but in this case a nine-year-old girl with one leg who’s just trying to live?

Jae brings her back to headquarters to try and figure out what to do, trusting his superior Karthik with the info, while Pavi sneaks off only to discover another Avatar — specifically, her twin sister Nisha (Aishu Devan). Shouts to Paramount for doing a good job hiding this secret despite it being pretty obvious that front-loading twins as the main characters of the series would imply they’re both the Avatar. Given what we find out shortly — that Nisha has a lot of Korra’s impulsiveness and anger in her, while Pavi has Aang’s wackiness while being all refusal no call — it’s a neat way of splitting and analyzing what made previous Avatars work (or not) thanks to the twins.

It also kicks us into our central mystery in Episode 2: Who are Pavi and Nisha, why don’t they remember each other, and how are they both the Avatar — the first time in the Avatar cycle that two people have held the title at the same time? Shades of Buffy and Faith on Buffy the Vampire Slayer, perhaps? Rewinding time, we get to see a little bit about how Nisha has been training in secret under the guidance of Karthik and desperately wants to go out and help. She gets her chance thanks to the aforementioned giant green storm.

While we get to see Ellora activate the Bending Brigade to mitigate the damage of the storm, which is pretty neat, the focus is on Pavi and Nisha, who eventually join together to help, only to be confronted by a strange red, pulsating diamond crackling with evil-looking energy. After it does something to Karthik’s commander, who fled at the sight of it, Pavi and Nisha manage to trap it, only for the diamond to envelop them, send them to another dimension, and then hit them with what are likely missing memories. The diamond then disappears, leaving behind red crystalline structures throughout the wrecked Ellora, and again it seems pretty clear that this may not be evil so much as something reaching out — likely from the Spirit World, and potentially even an aspect of Korra; TBD on that.

This brings us to Episode 3, which thanks to an opening title sequence laying out the plot in classic Avatar style — thank goodness; it was missed in the first two half-hours — feels like the first real episode of the show. The main thrust here is that Jae is completely melting down at keeping the secret of the re-emergence of the Avatar(s), while Pavi and Nisha are at odds over doing Avatar training with the surprise return of the Order of the White Lotus, a group of wise men and women who often will help guide the Avatar. This comes together when the three characters all calm what looks like an armadillo-camel that’s been corrupted by the red energy; it acts like a pill bug rolling around Ellora, and we’ve had armadillo-bears and armadillo-tigers before.

Here we get another key component of the series — the music . Jeremy Zuckerman returns after working on The Last Airbender and Legend of Korra, and he’s created a heart-aching, gorgeously poignant score for the series, particularly the theme that haunts Pavi and Nisha in the first two episodes. But it isn’t until Episode 3 when Pavi plays the theme on the kalimba that it becomes clear what the real purpose of the score is. Memory is spurred on by music, and the song we’ve been hearing for two episodes so far is actually a song that Pavi and Nisha’s mother used to sing to them, complete with lyrics. It’s a goose bump-inducing moment when this is revealed, as the duo sing together on instinct, calming the animal and sparking various memories.

If there’s a criticism to be made here, it’s that it’s hard to tell exactly where this is all headed. We do get an indication when Pavi and Nisha discuss needing to go find their parents, and if this is a more emotionally driven story than the world-ending stakes facing Aang, or the threats to Republic City — and sometimes the world — that plagued Korra, it should be an interesting swerve. The show already tugs at your heartstrings from the opening moments, so this viewer at least is invested in seeing Pavi and Nisha find happiness.

But we’re also three episodes in and have thus far encountered one (1) Haven, and even with the show just starting, you can feel time ticking away. It’s also laudable to deal with a climate apocalypse, but a green storm, a tornado, and a red diamond are not exactly the terrifying and complex villains this franchise is known for. Perhaps that’s coming: Demon-masked antagonists show up right at the end of the third episode, and likely will spur our three main characters to flee and explore more of the world, thus setting up our stakes. Maybe as our own world has gotten murkier and more confusing, the world of Avatar has as well. There’s no one evil bad guy you can defeat to save the world; it’s up to the next generation to fix things as best as they can.

These are minor quibbles when it feels so good to get back to this universe with new characters, new settings, dazzling animation, and soaring music. Welcome back, Avatar; yip yip.

Avatar Easter Eggs, References, and Connections

While most of the easter eggs and references in these episodes are pretty blatant, it might be helpful to lay some of them out for more casual viewers (or since it’s been, you know, well over a decade). Let’s start with the play about Korra performed by a bunch of kids in the town square of Ellora. Plays have been built in since “The Ember Island Players” debuted in The Last Airbender Season 3, showing off the adventures of the characters in the series via a ridiculous play titled “The Boy In The Iceberg.”

In Episode 2, Karthik reveals the lost history of the Avatars — everyone only knows Korra — and shows off a scroll depicting the older Aang with the dumb chin beard as seen in Legend of Korra, Avatar Kyoshi, and Avatar Roku. There are, FYI, a lot more Avatars than that, including some secret ones that were revealed in the Avatar Aang movie.

In Episode 3, we also get to see some pictures of previous members of the Order of the White Lotus. The beloved Iroh is right in the middle, with Jeong Jeong to his right and Pakku to his left — all three members of the Order during the time of The Last Airbender. Curiously, it’s harder to identify the waterbenders on the left and right side of the display; the woman all the way on the left could potentially be Katara, but she doesn’t have the icon’s little hair loops. Other waterbenders known to be part of the Order include: Ayunerak, aka Mama, who appeared in The Dawn of Yangchen novel and has never been seen visually; Kavik, also from The Dawn of Yangchen, who has a very handsome picture but doesn’t look like the guy on the right otherwise; Ivalu, from — you won’t believe this — The Dawn Of Yangchen; and Aupilaarjuk, who was from Kyoshi’s era and only appeared in the Avatar Legends role-playing game. Sadly not pictured on the wall of fame is crazy old Bumi, the earthbending King of Omashu.

Also of note? The entire Haven of Ellora seems to be laid out like the symbol for the Order, which certainly implies a lack of coincidence in the Avatars ending up there. That said, we have yet to see the other six Havens, so maybe they’re all laid out the same with their own divisions of the Order.

Less an easter egg than a nice, progressive note: Jae has a boyfriend named Datu (Topher Ngo). While things don’t go further than some embraces and a kiss on the cheek, this is a far cry from the surprising swerve of Korra and Asami getting together in the final seconds of Legend of Korra, a move that was lauded (yay representation!) and lambasted for its execution (the quickness and generally unclear way they “got together”). Baking in Jae and his boyfriend right in the third episode seems like a clear way to be more explicit about the inclusive world of Avatar. Similar to DiMartino and Konietzko stepping back and letting more racially appropriate voices write, direct, and act, this shows a welcome growth from where they were a decade ago; they’ve clearly been listening and learning.

Finally, let’s talk about that odd red diamond. The dark energy does seem to be some sort of conduit to, or from, the spirit world, and given that we don’t know what Korra did or how Pavi and Nisha connect to this — or why there hasn’t been an Avatar in centuries — it raises a lot of questions we’ll surely explore as the show continues. Let’s throw out a crazy idea here: What if this wasn’t Korra’s fault; what if was Aang’s ? This is something that was dealt with before in Legend of Korra, but there’s something about this energy that’s reminiscent of energybending, the forbidden practice that Aang used to take away Fire Lord Ozai’s bending at the conclusion of The Last Airbender. Is it possible Aang broke something there that Korra was trying to fix, rather than the other way around? This is pure speculation, but why not? We’ve got plenty of episodes to be way off about these theories.

articles.title: NieR Creator Yoko Taro Says He Would Retire From Making Video Games but Fear of Dementia Keeps Him Working
articles.summary: As reported by Denfaminicogamer, Nier creator Yoko Taro was asked if he had any current projects or plans to make a new game. He replied, “nothing really,” and confessed that “I’m done with working. I don’t want to do it anymore.”
articles.body:
NieR franchise creator Yoko Taro dropped a big revelation about his motivations for continuing to work and his thoughts on the future of Japan’s game industry. As reported by Denfaminicogamer , Taro was asked if he had any current projects or plans to make a new game. He replied “nothing really,” and confessed that “I’m done with working. I don’t want to do it anymore.”

On top of this, Taro revealed that he already achieved his life goal before he even made critically-acclaimed titles like NieR Automata. Taro's first game as director was 2003 PS2 title Drakengard (known as Drag-on Dragoon in Japan). “With Drakengard, the first game I was given the opportunity to direct, I was actually able to do almost everything the way I wanted,” he said, noting that he was able to release a game that “represented the best I could do at the time.”

“As a game otaku, I think the dream is to release something you’ve always wanted to create into the world. Having achieved that dream, I view everything after that as the remainder of my life,” he continued. Taro went on to reveal that he merely continued working because he’d be in trouble if he had no income.

Recently, he has considered retiring as he believes his savings and pension would be enough. However, he has a fear of developing dementia in old age, noting that he has heard of people being diagnosed with the disorder after retiring, and it is this fear that motivates him to keep working. So when he faces a difficult situation at work, he gets through it by telling himself: “This is good for preventing dementia.”

Taro made these revelations during a talk session with Ender Lilies and Ender Magnolia director Keisuke Okabe at The Tenth Mosaic video game culture festival held at the Tokyo French Institute last month. Of course, Taro is well-known for making eccentric and sometimes deadpan statements from under his ubiquitous Emil mask, so what he said should perhaps be taken with a grain of salt.

Regarding the future of the Japanese games industry, Taro quipped: “I’m going to die soon, so I really don’t care what happens to Japan’s game industry. However, I think that recently AI and various technologies have created a breeding ground where creators in their teens and 20s, who are even younger than Mr. Okabe, can freely create things.”

“I’m 56 now, but when people my age were young, we only had two options if we wanted to make a game: either ‘join a game company’ or ‘make a niche game for PC.’ If you wanted to make a 3D game you had no choice but to join a game company.” Taro said that the options for people who want to make games have broadened considerably since then, but this is inevitably leading to tougher competition.

“I think this competition will gradually spread like fire from the younger generations to the older generations of developers,” he commented. “As I’m already on the older side, I’m simply filled with fear and trepidation, hoping that these flames don’t reach me before I die.”

Regarding other titles and what motivates him to create games, Taro said “I don’t really get jealous of other games. When I come across something good, I end up viewing it from a fan’s perspective. This triggers my collector trait, and I just want to buy them all.”

“I’ve always worked in the games industry with the mindset of ‘filling in the gaps,’ he explained. “For example, I really like games like ICO and (Treasure’s bullet hell shooter) Ikaruga, but when I played them they were so perfect that I thought, ‘I don’t need to make games in these genres.’ That’s not jealousy, it’s the feeling of, ‘This gap has already been filled, so I need to fill a different one.’ I think the reason that my games are crude games full of terrible things is because the pioneers have already seized all the beautiful aspects.”

Since 2021’s Nier Reincarnation and the reboot of Nier Replicant, Taro has worked on the Voice of Cards RPG series and 2024 mobile title 404 GAME RE:SET. He is currently writing the upcoming as-yet untitled Neon Genesis Evangelion TV series , with NieR and Drakengard composer Keiichi Okabe providing the music.

Of course, Nier fans are desperate for a proper follow-up, but so far nothing has been announced. In November last year, the developer said he’d been working on various projects, but they just keep getting canceled .

“I often get told stuff like, ‘Why aren’t you making a new sequel to NieR?’ or, ‘Yoko Taro isn’t doing anything,’ but that’s because recently, a lot of projects I was involved in got discontinued midway through development," he said.

"I’ve actually been working on some stuff, it’s just that it never ended up seeing the light of day. I got paid for it, so I personally have no issues with that, but people seem to think that I haven’t been doing anything just because none of the work I’ve done is being released."

Verity Townsend is a Japan-based freelance writer who previously served as editor, contributor and translator for the game news site Automaton West. She has also written about Japanese culture and movies for various publications.

articles.title: Pokémon TCG's Delta Reign Expansion Is Finally Up For Preorder at Amazon and Target
articles.summary: Pokémon TCG Delta Reign preorders are now live at Amazon and Target, including Booster Bundles below market price, Elite Trainer Boxes, and 36-pack Display Boxes.
articles.body:
With all the buzz around Pokemon’s 30th Celebration expansion and extra bargains that came out during the Prime Day sale , waking up to see the first Amazon and Target listings for Delta Reign preorders was a surprise to be sure, but a welcome one.

Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution—Delta Reign Elite Trainer Box

Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution — Delta Reign Booster Bundle

Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution—Delta Reign Booster Display Box

Delta Reign Pokemon Center Elite Trainer Box (Exclusive)

For transparency, these aren’t listings by Amazon itself on the retailer site — but usual third-party sellers who operate on the same platform.

These are sellers we’ve found to still sell and deliver their stock just fine, but these listings all come with Amazon’s 30-day replacement/refund window if anything goes awry. "Kings Games" is a New York-based TCG store, and we've personally purchased from them ourselves to great success.

We currently don’t know when official Amazon-sold preorders for the Mega-Rayquaza-themed collection will go live, but in the meantime, all three big Delta Reign products we’ve seen are either close to market price — or actually undercutting it in one case.

Ahead of the expansion’s release date on 6 November, here are all three Delta Reign boxes you and other Pokemon TCG fans can pre-order and secure right now.

Delta Reign Booster Bundle Under Market Price

The biggest highlight of the Delta Reign’s preorder drop is the Booster Bundle, now priced at $74.95 on Amazon .

It’s surprising to see preorders for a Pokemon TCG Booster Bundle priced below $80 right out the gate, but what’s even more so is that this listing from seller Kings Games is that it’s undercutting TCGplayer’s estimated market price of $78.44. Keep in mind you wouldn’t get this on release day, though, with delivery currently set for November 10.

Along with that $3.89 subverting, Amazon is now beating any actual listings selling Delta Reign Booster Bundles on TCGplayer, too — with the lowest costing $77 .

There aren’t any preorders for individual Delta Reign booster packs live yet, but at $74.95 for this six-pack box, you’ll be paying around $12.49 per pack.

36-pack Booster Display Box For Just Under $270

articles.title: After Going Hands-On With the New Marvel Comics App, I Still Don't Know Why Unlimited Had to Die
articles.summary: Earlier this week, Marvel announced that it was discontinuing the Marvel Unlimited app, only to have it replaced by the new Marvel Comics app, powered by Webtoon. At New York Comic Con I had the chance to go hands-on with the app, and I am struggling to see why it needs to exist.
articles.body:
Earlier this week, Marvel announced that it was discontinuing the Marvel Unlimited app , only to have it replaced by the new Marvel Comics app, powered by Webtoon. At New York Comic Con , I had the chance to go hands-on with the app, and I am struggling to see why it needs to exist.

Just like Marvel Unlimited, the new Marvel Comics app will bring the entire Marvel and Star Wars comics libraries at both of its subscription tiers. On the surface, the big advantage Webtoon has over Unlimited is how quickly new comics will be available — with the more expensive ‘Ultimate’ tier getting new issues 30 days after print, rather than Unlimited’s 90-day waiting period.

Webtoon shared a rough roadmap for the app; it’s looking to bring in Disney and Pixar comics, make it easier to create your own custom lists, and create different profiles for all the comics readers in your home – even kids. But, Webtoon failed to share dates for when any of these improvements are coming, so at least for now, it looks like the bulk of the changes are minor cosmetic ones.

Marvel Comics Powered by Webtoon – Hands-On Photos

Webtoon said that its mission in designing this app was to make it faster and easier to use. After all, Unlimited has been around since 2007, and the UI still kind of looks like it’s stuck about a decade in the past. But rather than give Marvel Unlimited a facelift, the decision was made to create a brand new app. While the navigation does seem a bit more modernized, the app itself isn’t noticeably faster than Unlimited was. Of course, this could come down to the tablets at the Webtoon booth and spotty convention Wi-Fi, but I couldn’t really feel the difference.

Once you click into an issue, the Marvel Comics app does get a bit more compelling. Before you start reading the issue, it’ll bring you into a sort of overview page, where you’ll be able to see the information about the selected issue, but you’ll also be able to slide through other issues in the series on the top of the screen. There’s also a section where you’ll be able to see every reading guide that issue is a part of.

When I’m reading comics on the Unlimited app, I tend to make a beeline straight for reading guides, because I simply don’t have the patience to read entire comics runs that sometimes have hundreds of issues. Marvel Unlimited’s reading guides were excellent, and it seems like they’ve carried over to the Webtoon app. But, again, I only had a few minutes with the app in a crowded booth at NYCC, so I didn’t exactly have time to see if all of my favorite guides were intact.

Marvel Comics "Next Big Thing" Panel Art Gallery

Once you get into an actual comic, though, not much has changed. You can still choose between reading the entire page or reading panel by panel. With the latter option, you can also choose to have it zoom back out when you’re ready to move on to the next page, in order to appreciate all the art on the page, just the way you would in a regular comic.

That’s a great way to read digital comics, but Marvel Unlimited had the exact same options, and it wasn’t hard to set up. As nice as the new UI is, that probably could have been implemented with a hefty update, rather than asking all of the Marvel Unlimited users to switch over to a whole new app. The Marvel Comics app will let you move over your library and all of your reading progress, but I can only imagine that there are going to be people who stubbornly won’t make the migration. I just hope it was worth that risk.

The new Marvel Comics app launches November 16 with more than 35,000 digital comics. Marvel Unlimited will sunset on December 7, 2026.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Everything To Know About the PUBG MOBILE Brainrot Royale Pumpkin-themed Update
articles.body:
It’s October, which means two things: spooky season is here, and it’s time to celebrate. That’s something PUBG MOBILE knows all too well, because going live today is a brand new pumpkin-themed makeover to Brainrot Royale in Version 4.6. It comes with some anticipated new quality of life changes, as well as new event gameplay, limited-time rewards, more social interaction, and stronger collection progression. Familiar faces including Boneka Ambalabu, Brr Brr Patapim and Ballerina Cappuccina are along for the ride too. Let’s break down everything the new update has to offer.

Things get eerie with the epic new Ghost Ship, a new timed event that alternates with the Boss Room. When the event begins, a gigantic ship emerges from the mist and sails into the centre of the level, where it periodically locks onto Brainrots travelling along the conveyor belt and fires tracking Ghost Bullets at them. Those tracking bullets select their target, and if there’s a hit, then the Brainrot mutates into a Pumpkin Brainrot, a special Version 4.6-limited tier that’s yours for the taking. You can also collect Pumpkin Brainrot by smashing the Pumpkin Eggs found in the Boss Room. You can take them back to your base, or perhaps steal them from someone else. The choice is yours.

That’s not all the Ghost Ship event offers. Special updrafts occur during the event, which permit players to fly up onto the ship’s deck. It’s there they will discover the Pirate Captain’s Shop. In it, great booty awaits in the form of limited items and rewards. To get all that pirate plunder, you’ll need to get Pirate Coins.

The Ghost Ship’s arrival introduces Pirate Coins, a new event currency separate from the regular coins earned in Brainrot Royale. Stealing another player’s Brainrot, smashing eggs in the Boss Room, and purchasing or shooting Brainrots can all earn you Pirate Coins. Higher-level and rarer Brainrots and eggs drop more Pirate Coins, so there’s plenty of reason to hunt down the biggest rewards.

While collecting Brainrot has its own set of rewards and challenges, we know what you’re thinking: wouldn’t it be fun to become an actual Brainrot? Well, thanks to the addition of new themed items, that dream is now a possibility. With Pirate Coins, you can purchase the Brainrot Wand, which allows you to get into costume, disguising yourself as the new pumpkin-themed Brainrot. There’s also a Magic Broom, which allows players to fly freely around the level and even bring another player along for the ride. That’s not all, though. The broom also has a useful dash attack which can be used to knock down thieves, giving players a chance to chase them down and recover any Brainrots they’ve stolen.

“With Version 4.6, we wanted to build on the fun and unpredictability of Brainrot Royale while giving players a new culture-inspired experience to jump into,” says Rick Li, Producer of PUBG MOBILE and Deputy General Manager of Quantum Studio, LightSpeed Studios, Tencent Games. “The pumpkin-themed update brings new twists like the Ghost Ship and creates even more unexpected moments between players.”

The update also introduces the Star Upgrade system, which allows players to convert their extra Brainrots into a higher-star version. To do this, you’ll select two Brainrots of the same type and star level through the fusion system. Succeed and your Brainrot will get bigger, produce more Coins per second and become a more valuable collectible. If the fusion fails, don’t worry! You’ll get a success-rate bonus for your next attempt. Keep at it and you can eventually upgrade a Brainrot all the way to Meteor tier.

Version 4.6 is amping up the ways players can interact with each other in-game. Now, when you walk up to another player, you can view their profile card, add them as a friend, exchange popularity gifts or hand over one of your Brainrots. In gifting, you can send Brainrot directly to another player’s backpack or base, making it easier to share your collection with friends.

“World of Wonder gives us the opportunity to keep expanding the ways players can experience PUBG MOBILE, and Brainrot Royale is a great example of that,” says Vincent Wang, General Manager and Head of PUBG MOBILE Publishing, Tencent Games. “ As the ecosystem grows, we want to keep giving players new experiences while creating more opportunities for talented creators and studios to bring new ideas to PUBG MOBILE.”

There are also some valuable quality of life improvements, including a new backpack capacity limit. Your backpack can now hold up to 64 Brainrots, and once it’s full, you won’t be able to pick up any more until you organise your collection or sell lower-value ones to free up space. There’s more room to grow back at your Base, though, with Version 4.6 raising the Rebirth level cap by five additional levels. Players who’ve reached the cap can now progress through new levels, and each level unlocks another base slot, giving you more space for Brainrots and Coin-producing facilities.

So what are you waiting for? PUBG MOBILE’s Brainrot Royale Pumpkin-themed update is now live, and a world full of Ghost Ships, Pirate Coins, magic wands, brooms, are at your fingertips.

PUBG MOBILE’s Brainrot Royale pumpkin-themed update is available now in World of Wonder as part of Version 4.6. Download PUBG MOBILE for free on the App Store and Google Play Store , and follow the official World of Wonder social channels on Instagram , TikTok and YouTube for the latest updates and creator content. You can also visit the official PUBG MOBILE social channels on Facebook , Instagram , X and YouTube .

articles.title: Agent Coulson Actor Teases Link to Just-Announced Marvel TV Show, Zodiac
articles.summary: Agents of SHIELD star Clark Gregg, most famous for playing Agent Phil Coulson in the first Avengers movie, has teased his involvement with the just-announced Marvel TV show, Zodiac.
articles.body:
Agents of SHIELD star Clark Gregg, most famous for playing Agent Phil Coulson in the first Avengers movie, has teased his involvement with the just-announced Marvel TV show, Zodiac.

Marvel announced Zodiac at a New York Comic Con panel yesterday with a logo, below, a 2028 release window, and little else. We know it's a spy thriller and, based on the logo, it has something to do with SHIELD. Hot on the heels of the reveal, Gregg shared the announcement to his Instagram , sparking speculation that the two shows are linked.

The logo for the show features the show’s title, Zodiac, with a stylized “o” and a stylized “a.” The “a” has a little eagle head in the middle, mirroring the SHIELD logo.

"For anyone who knows the comics, if you look closely at this title design, you’ll see a few clues about where we’re going," Marvel TV head Brad Winderbaum told the audience during the announcement. "I can’t tell you anything else about it yet because it’s a secret. We're going to start casting it in a couple weeks.”

Agents of SHIELD ended back in 2020 and saw Gregg’s Agent Coulson return from beyond the grave in android form. However, the series is not listed on the Disney+ "MCU Complete Timeline" section, which features every single canon MCU movie, TV series, and one-off special, so its place in official Marvel canon is unclear.

Chloe Bennet, who played Daisy, recently said she's "still low-key angry" that Agents of SHIELD isn't considered fully part of MCU canon — though has insisted she would reprise her role if asked. Fans are hoping to see the return of Samuel L. Jackson’s Nick Fury in Zodiac, which is named after a criminal organization made up of bad guys named after zodiac signs. Nick Fury’s brother, Scorpio, is one of them.

Marvel's Agents of SHIELD: The Many Lives (and Deaths) of Phil Coulson

Of course, there’s been no official word on where Zodiac will go. All we know is that it’s a spy thriller, and if it goes in another direction to the comics, it wouldn’t be the first time for the MCU.

Elsewhere in Marvel TV shows, Daredevil: Born Again will end with Season 3 . Ahead of that wrapping up, VisionQuest is landing on Disney+ on October 14, and the showrunners said they didn’t pay much attention to the wider MCU when putting the story together.

VisionQuest sees Paul Bettany reprise his role as Vision on the run from people seeking to weaponize him. The limited series will be eight episodes long. In case you missed it, here's everything announced at the Marvel TV and Animation panel at NYCC 2026 .
